oneliner.t: Republican dentist from Flagstaff who has served in the U.S. House since January 2011 (AZ-1, then AZ-4, now AZ-9). The House censured him in November 2021. Trump-endorsed, he was unopposed in the July 21, 2026 primary and faces Democrat Danielle Sterbinsky on Nov. 3.

hometown.t: Pinedale, Wyoming (raised there; Pinedale High School, 1977)

profile.residence: Bullhead City, AZ (listed address); see roots note

upbringing.t: Born in Rock Springs and raised in Pinedale, Wyoming, the eldest of ten children (seven sons, three daughters) of Republican parents; his grandparents were Slovenian and Basque immigrants. He earned a B.S. (1981) and a D.D.S. (1985) at Creighton University in Omaha, then ran a dental practice in Flagstaff from 1989 until his 2010 election, served as Arizona Dental Association president (2004–05), and had never held elected office before 2010. His brother Pete Gosar is a former Wyoming Democratic Party chair, and six siblings appeared in 2018 ads backing his Democratic opponent; their actions are theirs, not his.

platform.t: His House biography says he pursues more individual liberty and less government, and lists illegal immigration, border security and government spending as focuses. He did not fill out Ballotpedia's 2026 survey and published no 2026 platform in sources opened.
Co-led, with former Rep. Ann Kirkpatrick, legislation enabling Resolution Copper's mine near Superior (Oak Flat land exchange); opposed by environmental groups and the San Carlos Apache Tribe.
Voted in 2023 for H.Con.Res. 21 directing removal of U.S. troops from Syria; in Oct. 2022 invited Zelenskyy and Putin to Arizona for peace talks.

record.t: Elected in 2010 and serving since Jan. 3, 2011.

claims.claim: Owned his dental practice and was a Flagstaff small businessman for 25 years before his 2010 election.

record.t: He was a dentist in Flagstaff, but Wikipedia dates the practice 1989–2010, about 21 years, not 25.

claims.claim: Came to Congress with no prior political experience.

record.t: Wikipedia says he had never held elected office before 2010; his prior leadership roles were in dental associations.

claims.claim: Serving his seventh term in Congress.

record.t: True for the 118th Congress (2023–25), when the page was apparently written. He has served since 2011 and is now in his eighth term (elected to the 112th Congress and seven succeeding ones).

claims.claim: Chairman of the Congressional Western Caucus for the 115th and 116th Congresses.

record.t: Wikipedia lists him as Western Caucus chair among caucus memberships but sources opened do not give the Congresses.

claims.claim: Recognized by GovTrack as one of the most effective members of Congress.

record.t: No ranking, year or GovTrack page is given; GovTrack was not opened.

claims.claim: Chairman of the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations.

record.t: Committee rosters were not opened; Wikipedia confirms his committee seats were restored after the 2022 election but does not list this chairmanship.

entries.t: Asked AG Barr (with 26 other Republicans) for a special counsel on 2020 'irregularities'; made claims about Arizona voting machines, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania that Wikipedia describes as false; called Biden an 'illegitimate usurper'; co-led the Arizona objection on Jan. 6, 2021.

entries.t: PolitiFact's scorecard shows two rated statements, one False and one Pants on Fire: a Nov. 2022 tweet saying the law barred Secretary of State Katie Hobbs from overseeing the election she was running in, and a Jan. 2020 post of a photo said to show Obama shaking hands with Hassan Rouhani. The page did not show which rating went with which statement.
Voted to support Israel after the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack (per Wikipedia; roll call compiled separately).

effectiveness.note: His House biography (written for the 118th Congress) lists Natural Resources (chair, Oversight and Investigations subcommittee) and Oversight and Government Reform; 119th-Congress assignments were not confirmed. He has co-shared deanship of the Arizona delegation with David Schweikert since March 2025 (Wikipedia).

groups.name: Second Amendment, Taiwan, Interstate 11 (co-chair), Inventions (co-chair) caucuses

democracy.t: Co-led (with Sen. Ted Cruz) the objection to Arizona's electoral votes and voted Yea; it failed 121–303.
Voted Yea on the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes; it failed 138–282.

Promoted claims about the 2020 election that Wikipedia describes as false (faulty Arizona machines, a Wisconsin vote 'dump', dead voters in Pennsylvania), demanded a Maricopa County audit, compared Stop the Steal to the Alamo and called Biden an 'illegitimate usurper.'

Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said in a since-deleted video that he planned pressure on Congress with Gosar, Biggs and Mo Brooks; Gosar's office did not respond. Reported on Jan. 19, 2021 to have sought a pardon from Trump; none was granted. These are reports, not findings.
Wrote in his newsletter that in a 'better society' Gen. Mark Milley would be hung, blaming him for Guard delays on Jan. 6; House testimony he cited did not mention Milley. No formal action followed.

debates.note: Did not respond to Clean Elections debate invitations (Aug. 27, 2026 forum went ahead with Sterbinsky alone). Not counted as a formal decline.

note.t: Moved to Flagstaff by 1989 (dental practice). Wikipedia reports he listed a Prescott apartment as his official residence while keeping his Flagstaff home as primary (earning tax breaks), and in 2021 claimed a Bullhead City condo for AZ-9 while public records showed the Flagstaff home.

checks.legal: Courts: CourtListener and Justia unreachable from this environment (fetch tool refused). Wikipedia reports no criminal or civil case against him. Ethics: House censure confirmed in the Clerk's roll-call record; ethics.house.gov not reachable; Wikipedia reports a Campaign for Accountability complaint over proxy voting during CPAC (2021) with no outcome stated.
checks.foreign: Financial disclosures not opened (no PDF located). FARA not searched. Nothing foreign found in sources reviewed.
checks.claims: Campaign site refused by the fetch tool; mechanical sample = every checkable claim on his official House biography (7 rated: 2 true, 2 partly, 3 unverifiable). No 2026 ads found in coverage. PolitiFact scorecard: 1 False, 1 Pants on Fire (statements on Katie Hobbs overseeing the 2022 election, Nov. 2022, and a photo of Obama with Rouhani, Jan. 2020); the page did not map ratings to statements, so they are not scored here.
checks.democracy: Clerk roll calls 10 and 11 of 2021 read directly; Wikipedia and KJZZ for statements. Not checked: Jan. 6, 2017 and Jan. 6, 2025 counts, and the Dec. 2020 Texas v. Pennsylvania amicus list.

legal.t: The House adopted H.Res. 789 censuring him (223–207; Democrats 221–0, Republicans 2–207 with Cheney and Kinzinger voting yes and one present) for posting an edited anime video depicting his likeness attacking figures resembling Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and President Biden. The resolution removed him from the Oversight and Natural Resources committees. He called it an attack on his First Amendment rights and re-posted the video; his committee seats were restored after Republicans won the House in 2022.
legal.status: Censure adopted Nov. 17, 2021; committee seats restored after 2022 election

research_notes: CENSURE: Clerk roll 379 confirms date, tally and party split; the Rules Committee page confirms the manager's amendment removing him from Oversight and Natural Resources. A Sept. 2023 KJZZ/Cronkite piece dates the censure to 2022; the Clerk record shows Nov. 17, 2021. An amendment by then-Rep. Raúl Grijalva (to remove him only from Natural Resources) was withdrawn. EXTREMISM REPORTING (Wikipedia, single secondary source): keynote at Nick Fuentes's AFPAC (Feb. 26, 2021); later told CPAC there is no room for violence; employs Wade Searle, reportedly a Fuentes follower, as digital director; an Oath Keepers leader attributed a 'civil war' remark to him that his office did not confirm. These are reports of association and speech, not legal findings. FAMILY: his siblings' political ads (2018, 2020) and brother Pete's Democratic career are their own. Track AIPAC: $18,250 with no AIPAC PAC listed. Primary July 21, 2026: 79,336 votes, unopposed. 2024 general: 65.3%. Photo not retrieved.
